front: What does the autonomic nervous system do?
back: Regulates the function of the internal organs and works involuntarily.

front: How does the neuromuscular system work?
back: The nervous system and muscles work together to allow movement. Changes take place before, during and after exercise. Uses the sympathetic, parasympathetic and central nervous systems.

front: What is the overall role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems?
back: To transmit information from the brain to body parts that need to adjust their activity in preparation for exercise.

front: What does the sympathetic nervous system do to the body?
back: Prepares the body for exercise through the "fight or flight" response.

front: What does the parasympathetic nervous system do to the body?
back: Relaxes the body and slows energy functions through the "rest and relax" response.

front: What are the three main types of muscle fibre?
back: Slow oxidative (Type I) - slow twitch; Fast oxidative glycolytic (Type IIa) - medium twitch; Fast glycolytic (Type IIb) - fast twitch.

front: What part of the body contains all three muscle fibre types?
back: Skeletal muscles. The proportion of each fibre type is genetically determined.

front: What muscle fibre type would an elite marathon runner have the majority of?
back: Slow oxidative (Type I) fibres.

front: What are the features of slow oxidative fibres (Type I)?
back: Slow to contract; fatigue slowly; high in mitochondria and myoglobin; rich capillary supply.

front: What sports are slow oxidative fibres used for?
back: Endurance events.

front: What are the features of fast oxidative glycolytic fibres (Type IIa)?
back: Produce energy through both aerobic and anaerobic processes; moderate number of mitochondria; fast recovery; fatigue resistant; adaptable through training.

front: What are the features of fast glycolytic fibres (Type IIb)?
back: Fast contraction speed; fatigue quickly; low mitochondria and oxidative capacity; produce quick bursts of speed.

front: What sports are fast glycolytic fibres used for?
back: Sprinting and high jump.

front: What are the effects of training on muscle fibres?
back: Muscle fibre type is genetically determined, but fibres can increase in size through hypertrophy, resulting in greater strength.

front: What are muscle fibres grouped into?
back: Motor units.

front: What does a motor unit consist of?
back: A motor neuron and the muscle fibres it controls.

front: How many muscle fibre types can be found in one motor unit?
back: Only one type. A motor unit is either slow twitch or fast twitch.

front: How does a contraction occur in a motor unit?
back: Muscle fibres work with the nervous system to produce movement.

front: What do motor units transmit and where to?
back: Nerve impulses to muscle fibres.

front: What are the physical features of a motor neuron?
back: Branches that end at neuromuscular junctions on muscle fibres.

front: What are muscles made up of?
back: Many motor units of varying sizes.

front: What is found in a motor unit within a small muscle?
back: Only a few muscle fibres per motor neuron.

front: What is found in a motor unit within a large muscle?
back: A motor neuron controlling hundreds of muscle fibres.

front: What is the all-or-none law?
back: Once stimulated, either all muscle fibres in a motor unit contract or none contract.

front: What is not possible for a motor unit to do?
back: Partially contract.

front: What is the threshold?
back: The minimum level of stimulation required to initiate a contraction.

front: What happens if impulses are equal to or greater than the threshold?
back: All fibres in the motor unit contract.

front: What happens if impulses are below the threshold?
back: No muscle contraction occurs.

front: What is wave summation?
back: Repeated activation of a motor neuron stimulates a muscle fibre, producing a greater force of contraction.

front: What is the first stage of wave summation?
back: Each nerve impulse causes calcium to be released within the muscle cell.

front: What happens if nerve impulses are repeated without time to relax?
back: Calcium accumulates, causing a forceful, sustained contraction called a tetanic contraction.

front: What is a tetanic contraction?
back: A smooth, sustained contraction caused by repeated nerve impulses and calcium buildup.

front: What is spatial summation?
back: The recruitment of additional and larger motor units to increase force production.

front: How does spatial summation work?
back: Impulses are received simultaneously at different points on a neuron and combine to activate more motor units.

front: What does PNF stand for?
back: Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation.

front: What is PNF?
back: An advanced stretching technique used to increase flexibility and range of motion.

front: What is the most practical PNF technique?
back: CRAC: Contract - Relax - Antagonist - Contract.

front: What are proprioceptors?
back: Sensory organs in muscles, tendons and joints that detect movement and body position.

front: What are the two types of proprioceptors?
back: Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs.

front: What do muscle spindles detect?
back: Changes in muscle length.

front: What do Golgi tendon organs detect?
back: The amount of force or tension being applied to a muscle.

front: Where are muscle spindles located?
back: Between muscle fibres.

front: What information do muscle spindles provide to the CNS?
back: Information about how far and how fast a muscle is being stretched. These are excitatory signals.

front: What happens after the CNS receives information from muscle spindles?
back: The CNS sends an impulse back to the muscle, causing it to contract and triggering the stretch reflex.

front: What is the purpose of the stretch reflex?
back: To prevent overstretching and reduce the risk of injury by causing the muscle to contract.

front: Where are Golgi tendon organs located?
back: Between the muscle fibre and tendon.

front: What happens during PNF when a muscle contracts isometrically?
back: Golgi tendon organs detect increased tension and send inhibitory signals to the brain.

front: What is the result of these inhibitory signals?
back: The antagonist muscle relaxes and lengthens through a process called autogenic inhibition.
